title: Looking back: year three
hook: the great story, the disciples, the roads, the teachers
tomorrow: free yourself first, or stay until everyone is free?

segments.voice: Yesterday, year two: his own words, and the Kalamas told to know for themselves. Today, year three, the great story, and the people in it.
screen: `HIS OWN WORDS.` → `YEAR THREE: THE GREAT STORY.`

segments.voice: Some of the best advice people ever get comes from someone who says, up front, I'm no expert. Year three told the great story: the life, the disciples, the roads, the teachers. And there's an odd detail in it. Two seekers, Sariputta and Moggallana, had a pact: whoever finds the deathless first tells the other. One morning Sariputta sees a monk on his alms round, Assaji, so calm it stops him. Who's your teacher, he asks, and what does he teach? Assaji's answer: I'm new. I've only just gone forth. I can't teach it at length. A beginner, saying so. That's who brings the Buddha his two chief disciples.
screen: `"I'M NO EXPERT."` → `A PACT BETWEEN TWO SEEKERS.` → `ASSAJI: "I'M NEW."`

segments.voice: So why does the Vinaya hand this turn to a beginner? Look at what Assaji does next. He doesn't refuse, and he doesn't pretend. He offers what he has, the gist, in one short verse: of things that arise from a cause, the Tathagata has told the cause, and also how they end. That's all. Sariputta hears it, and the text says the clear eye of the teaching opens in him. He runs to Moggallana, who sees at once that something has changed. Sariputta repeats the verse, and the same thing happens again. The two go to the Buddha together, and in the Vinaya the Buddha, seeing them come, says these two will be his chief pair of disciples. Here's the puzzle solved. The teaching didn't need an expert to travel. It needed someone who had tasted it and passed on the piece he had. A later commentary adds that Sariputta honored Assaji all his life. That's the great story's quiet engine: not only the Buddha, but the disciples, handing it on, hand to hand. The great story is still being told that way.
screen: `ONE SHORT VERSE: THE CAUSE, THE END.` · `SARIPUTTA HEARS. MOGGALLANA HEARS.` · `"THESE TWO WILL BE MY CHIEF PAIR."` · `PASSED HAND TO HAND.` · then, large: `THE GREAT STORY.`

segments.voice: Count the teachers you've had on this path, and not only the famous ones: a book, a grandparent, a friend who said one sentence at the right time. Touch a finger for each one. When you run out of names, stay with the last one for the rest of the sit, and let yourself be grateful for the piece they passed on.
Looking back, at year three: the great story, and the beginner whose one verse sent the Buddha two great disciples.
For the road: the great story, carried by beginners as much as by masters. Three of fourteen.

howItsDone: Buddhists honor the teachers who passed the dhamma on to them; in temples the Buddha's two chief disciples, Sariputta and Moggallana, are often shown standing on either side of him.

fork.setup: a coworker asks how you keep steady on deadline days. you've only practiced a little while yourself. what does Assaji's answer suggest?
options: say you're still new, then share the one thing that has helped you.
say nothing until you've practiced for years; beginners mislead.
explain the whole path in detail so you sound like you know it.
fork.reveal: Assaji did both: 'i'm new', then the gist. one honest verse was enough to start the great story's next chapter.

original.note: Pali: cause; the key word in Assaji's verse, about things that arise from a cause.

what a scholar hears: the Vinaya tells it; Assaji was among the Buddha's first five monks, yet in this telling he still calls himself new.

chat.meaning: In the Vinaya, Assaji admits he is new, then shares one verse; that verse brings the Buddha his two chief disciples.

tie.story: Assaji told Sariputta he was new, then gave him one verse, and it changed Sariputta and Moggallana.
tie.friend: Mai can be honest that she's still learning and teach the kid the one thing she does well.
tie.you: what small piece could you pass on this week?

Sariputta.meaning: one of the Buddha's two chief disciples

Moggallana.meaning: Sariputta's friend, the other of the two chief disciples

Assaji.meaning: an early monk whose one verse reached Sariputta

Vinaya.meaning: the texts of monastic discipline, with stories of the early community

Tathagata.meaning: the thus-gone one: a title the Buddha used for himself

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.23-24 (Sariputta and Moggallana meet Assaji and go to the Buddha)
commentarial tradition (Sariputta's lifelong honor for Assaji)

notes: Mahavagga 1.23 paraphrased: Assaji says he is new, not long gone forth, and cannot teach at length, but can give the meaning in brief; the verse (ye dhamma hetuppabhava...) paraphrased, not quoted; Sariputta gains the 'stainless eye of the dhamma'; Moggallana notices his changed look; at 1.24 the Buddha says they will be a chief pair (aggasavakayuga). Confirm.
Assaji as one of the first five monks (pañcavaggiya): standard; confirm that this is the same Assaji.
'A later commentary adds that Sariputta honored Assaji all his life' (the commentaries tell that he slept with his head toward wherever Assaji was staying). Confirm the source before release.
The howItsDone line on images of the two chief disciples flanking the Buddha is a common temple arrangement; 'often' kept soft. Confirm.
Shape: puzzle (why does the Vinaya give this turn to a self-declared beginner?). Mai's storyline: a younger kid at the youth group asks her to teach drawing.
Surprising fact: the Buddha's two chief disciples came to him through one short verse from a monk who said he was new.
